# Project Instructions

This workspace supports preparation of an EB1A RFE response, including organizing evidence and drafting supporting materials. Follow these instructions for all work in the project.

## Accuracy and Evidence

- Treat user-provided documents and primary sources as authoritative. Do not invent facts, dates, citation counts, credentials, quotations, or legal requirements.
- Keep factual statements traceable to a source. Flag missing, conflicting, or unverified information instead of filling gaps with assumptions.
- Preserve the meaning of source documents when summarizing or editing. Clearly distinguish source facts from proposed wording, analysis, and open questions.
- Do not describe assistance as legal advice or make guarantees about USCIS outcomes. Keep legal conclusions and filing decisions with the user's attorney.

## Independent Citation Record

- Follow `Independent Citation Record/Independent Citation Record Guide.md` when preparing citation-record materials.
- Use the user's Google Scholar profile as the primary source for citation totals and citing-paper lists, consistent with the guide. Record the source URL and dated snapshot for any figures reported.
- A citation is independent only when the citing paper and cited paper share no authors. Verify author lists before classifying a citation; do not infer independence from title or institution alone.
- Per the user's instruction, papers authored by the PI (Richard D. Cummings) or the former PI (Umesh R. Desai) are self-citations and are never counted as independent, even on papers that the user did not co-author.
- "Desai" and "Cummings" are common surnames. Match authors on surname plus initials, never surname alone. When surnames collide but initials are unavailable for comparison, flag the entry for manual review instead of counting or excluding it.
- Google Scholar truncates author lists with an ellipsis. Resolve the full list from Google Scholar itself: the cited paper's profile article page (`#gsc_oci_table`) and, for citing entries, the BibTeX record behind that result's "Cite" control. Do not substitute CrossRef or another third-party database as the primary basis for independence.
- **Scholar's BibTeX is itself abbreviated**, with `and others`, on long papers — so "we read the Cite popup" is not by itself a complete list. The capture records that case honestly as `full_authors` populated **and** `truncated = true`, with `resolution = "resolved but Scholar shows 'and others'"`. Measured 2026-11-03: 196 active rows have both, and all 19 queued rows that have a BibTeX list are of this abbreviated kind. What keeps an abbreviated list off an exhibit is the corroboration stage, which derives `confirm_state` from `!truncated` and demotes an incomplete INDEPENDENT to REVIEW — **not** `name-match.evaluateEntry`, which returns INDEPENDENT whenever `full_authors` is non-empty without consulting `truncated`. Verified 2026-11-03 that **0 highlighted rows** rest on an abbreviated list without a complete external or human basis. Reordering those two branches is **not** a no-op — it changes the intermediate status of 534 of 4021 entries — so it is a rule change to discuss with the user, not a cleanup. `popup_sample` is kept to 400 chars, so `and others` usually cannot be re-derived from the saved sample; read `resolution` instead.
- Per the user's instruction, corroborate each candidate independent citation against an external record that publishes the complete author list (PubMed via NCBI E-utilities, then OpenAlex) before highlighting it. Google Scholar stays primary. Record the external source and link. A paper indexed in neither service may still be highlighted when Scholar's own list is complete, but flag it for a spot-check.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-02, an external record settles a row rather than merely shadowing it: where a complete external author list shares an author with the cited paper or lists either PI, the row is dependent, and where it shares nobody it clears a Scholar byline that the page truncated. This supersedes the earlier rule that an external disagreement only downgraded a row to manual review and that no entry was ever promoted on an external record alone. Both transitions live in one place, `tools/corroboration.js`, called by the live capture and by `tools/reapply-corroboration.js` — never reimplement the state change in either caller.
- Believe an external record only when it is the same work. A title match must clear a credibility test before it can set a row's state (`titleMatchIsCredible` in `tools/crosscheck.js`): about 80% of the longer title's words, or a shorter side of at least four words wholly contained, or a leading prefix of at least **three** words, since Scholar truncates a long title with an ellipsis. Never accept a match on a one- or two-word fragment — a lone surname, an instrument acronym, or a journal name Scholar mistook for a title will match an unrelated paper. The prefix floor was two until 2026-11-02, which re-admitted exactly that class: `"[CITATION] Structural Biology"` matched the unrelated `"Structural biology of allergens"`. Measured over the settled corpus the raise to three costs nothing — only three rows rested on a prefix and all three had three words or more. Discarding an invalid match is not a policy change: it removes evidence that was never valid and the row falls back to whatever Scholar's own list supports, with `external_match_credible = 0` recorded and any byline the bad match overwrote restored to Scholar's own.
- Google Scholar prefixes some citing rows with a bracketed link-type marker — `[CITATION]`, `[BOOK]`, `[TXT]`. It is part of Scholar's rendering and **not part of the title**, and it is never evidence of anything about the work itself: not of a preprint, not of a non-English entry, and not of being unindexed. Stripping it happens in one place, `tools/scholar-marker.js`, used by the external look-up string and by `paperKey`. Leaving it in was the artifact behind most of the "Nothing indexes it" bucket: the word "citation" travelled into the PubMed and OpenAlex query, so no record could ever match. Only a leading marker on the allowlist is removed — a chemistry title's own brackets, as in `"...Benzopyrano[4,3-e][1,2,4]triazolo..."`, are the compound name and must survive.
- A look-up that did not complete is **not** a finding that a paper is unindexed. Throttled or failed requests used to fall through to `unverified-coverage`, which is a settling state, so an OpenAlex rate limit silently manufactured countable evidence. `tools/crosscheck.js` now retries 429 and 5xx honouring `Retry-After` and reports `{ unknown: true }`; `capture-citations.js` files that outcome as `confirm_state = 'lookup-failed'`, which is deliberately **not** settling, and demotes an INDEPENDENT row back to REVIEW. `tools/refetch-corroboration.js` exits non-zero when any look-up failed, so a throttled sweep fails loudly instead of quietly settling rows — re-run it until it exits 0 rather than accepting a partial pass.
- Honour `Retry-After` only up to a ceiling (`RETRY_MAX_WAIT_MS`, 60s in `tools/crosscheck.js`); beyond it, abandon the row as an incomplete look-up. Waiting a hint literally is not a retry: the anonymous OpenAlex pool answered `Retry-After: 44969` (~12.5h) on 2026-11-03 and the sweep sat in one sleep emitting pacing lines, indistinguishable from a slow run. Abandoning is the honest outcome because the caller leaves the row alone and fails loudly.
- Credentials for the external look-ups live in `.env` at the repository root (git-ignored; `.env.example` is the tracked template) and are loaded by `tools/env.js` at require time, so a key never has to appear on a command line where it would land in shell history or a recorded scrollback. A variable already set in the real environment wins. **An OpenAlex key is effectively required**, not optional: the anonymous pool throttles a corroboration sweep into a twelve-hour wait, while the same request with a key returns 200.
- Send an OpenAlex key as an `Authorization: Bearer` header, **never** as an `api_key` query parameter, even though both are accepted. `getJson` records a failed request as `${msg} :: ${url}` and that note can be written into a report JSON that ships in the evidence folder, so a credential in a URL would be filed with it. Never log a credential value anywhere; `crosscheck.credentialSummary()` prints the names in play only, and a run logs it at start and warns when no OpenAlex key is present.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-03, **a re-look-up targets the review queue and nothing else** — `refetch-corroboration.js` scopes to `tally.isReviewQueue` by default, so it never re-queries a row the packet has already settled. This is right on the merits, not merely smaller: a queued row is undecided so new evidence can only resolve it, while a counted row is filed evidence whose mark a fresh query could silently change. Measured the same day, the old default (marker rows, any status) reached 58 rows of which **34 were already highlighted**, and an earlier such run moved the packet total from 1047 to 1049 independent — a sweep that can move a filed figure is not a cleanup. Widening still exists (`--widen=marker`, `--widen=unindexed`, since the marker bug did affect counted rows) but each prints a warning naming that counted rows are in scope. `--all-unindexed` remains as the old spelling of `--widen=unindexed`.
- External author names are normalised to natural order at look-up time (`toDisplayName` in `tools/crosscheck.js`). PubMed returns "Surname, Given" and the list is stored as one comma-joined string, so an inverted name tore into a phantom bare surname plus a given name — 21 of 692 rows, and it flipped a correctly DEPENDENT row to REVIEW when the phantom surname collided with a real author. Never reassemble a stored byline by guessing where a comma belongs; `--repair-names` re-reads an affected row from the service instead. Of those 21 rows only one is still classified REVIEW and none is on the queue, so repairing them cannot move a filed figure — re-derive the set with a read-only query against the store, and `tornAuthors` is the detector.
- A **discarded** external match (`external_match_credible = 0`) keeps its `external_source` as the audit trail of the rejection but its URL is never published. The link points at a different paper — cit-001476's PubMed hit is a swine-lung article that scored 0.07 against a `Glycoproteomics` byline — and the dashboard JSON ships with the packet, so hiding it at render time while the data still carries it is not enough. `externalUrl(r)` in `tools/build-dashboard-data.js` is the one gate, applied to every projection out of the store (`review_queue`, `allWorks`, `language_held`/unsettled), and `tools/build-review-sheet.js` blanks the same column. Adding a new listing means routing through that helper, not reading `external_url` directly.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-02, a row the rules cannot settle is resolved by a person through `tools/apply-decision.js` (`--row=cit-000082 --verdict=dependent --write --reprint --rebuild`, or fill `your_decision` in the review CSV and pass `--from-csv`). A human decision is its own basis, `confirm_state = 'user-decided'`, reported separately as "settled by you" and never folded into "externally confirmed", so a packet figure can state how much of it rests on a person's reading. `tally.js` treats it as settling a row, and `copyReliability` ranks a decided copy of a duplicated paper above any machine reading.
- A decision is written into the per-page report JSON and the store is rebuilt from it; never `UPDATE` `Database/citation-catalog.sqlite` to record one, since the next `tools/build-catalog.js` silently reverts it and a store that disagrees with the reports is the state `tools/build-ledger.js` exits non-zero on. `apply-decision.js` resolves the `row_uid` against the store, locates the entry in its report, and refuses the whole batch unless the title at that position matches — editing a citation nobody asked about is worse than refusing. It is dry-run by default, backs up what it touches to `Exhibits/Supporting/Pre-decision-<date>/`, writes atomically, and `--revert` restores the exact pre-decision state. It does not re-fetch from Scholar: the user's reading of the published article is the evidence, and `decided_by`/`decided_on`/`decided_note` record who and why.
- A decision cannot override the language screen. Per the 2026-11-01 no-translation decision, classifying a non-English row as independent leaves it unhighlighted and out of the totals; the tool says so rather than letting the user infer it from a total that did not move.
- Keep citation counts and percentages tied to a dated Google Scholar snapshot. Identify the source and snapshot date whenever reporting totals.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-10-30, independent and dependent counts must be kept in a log usable for both per-article and global statistics. Run `tools/build-ledger.js` after every batch and quote figures from `Exhibits/Supporting/citation-ledger-<snapshot>.csv` (and its `.json`) rather than recomputing them; each run also appends a line to `citation-ledger-history.csv`. Do not maintain a parallel tally: `tools/tally.js` holds the single definition of what counts, and a publication contributes only while its exhibit PDF is filed.
- PENDING USER CONFIRMATION (2026-11-02 — a wording change to the bullet above, flagged rather than quietly applied): the bullet still stands, quote from the dated CSV and never recompute by hand. What changed is which artifact holds the rows. `Database/citation-catalog.sqlite` is the primary durable store of the citation rows and must not be deleted; `tools/build-ledger.js` reads the active rows out of it and its CSV is a **derived report** of those rows, while still recomputing the same figures independently from the report JSON as a cross-check. A disagreement between the two is a defect to investigate, is resolved in neither side's favour, and both tools exit non-zero and write nothing — so do not quote any figure from a run that failed, and do not "fix" it by picking the number you prefer.
- Refer to a citation row by its `row_uid` (`cit-000106`), never by the integer `id`. The uid is minted once, never reused, and still means the same row after a re-capture or a rebuild; `id` is a frozen legacy alias. Every listing from `tools/query-catalog.js` leads with it. A row whose exhibit is archived or re-captured is retired with `superseded_at` and a reason, never deleted, and `tools/build-catalog.js` merges into the store rather than replacing it — run it without `--write` first to see the plan.
- `Database/Backups/` holds the verified pre-write snapshots the builder takes. Keep them on disk as the recovery path; do not commit them (they are several megabytes each and a new one appears on nearly every run) and do not delete them to save space. The tracked durable copy is `Database/citation-catalog.sqlite` itself.
- For non-English citations, do not treat machine translation as certified. Follow the guide's requirement for a human translator fluent in both languages and an accompanying certification/affidavit; otherwise exclude those entries from highlighted and adjusted English-only totals.
- Per the user's decision on 2026-11-01, no translations will be obtained. Non-English entries stay unhighlighted and the packet reports an adjusted independent total and percentage based solely on English citations, which is the guide's second path. The guide's test is whether an entry is "listed in English", meaning its title, author list and venue, not its body — so a foreign-language abstract under an English title is not evidence of a non-English entry.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-03, a non-English entry is **not on the review queue** — it belongs in the Non-English listing only (`cit-000077` was the example). The queue is the list where reading the published byline settles something, and with no translations being obtained no reading of such a row can change the packet, so it is not work. The single definition is `isReviewQueue` in `tools/tally.js` (`status === 'REVIEW'` and no language flag); `v_review`, `v_pub_stats`, `tools/build-ledger.js`, `tools/build-review-sheet.js`, `tools/query-catalog.js` and the dashboard all mirror that one condition. Keep both figures: `review` counts every REVIEW row so the status partition still sums to `records`, while `review_queue` is the sheet length — today 72 and 67. Never delete the excluded count; it stays in `review_non_english`, in `flagged_non_english`, and in `v_non_english`.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-03, **the language screen supersedes a row's other classifications**: "if language is non-english that should supersede any other flags like independent … we should collapse them into non-English." So `isIndependentPending` in `tools/tally.js` requires no language flag, and a non-English row is reported once, under the non-English bucket, never as unsettled independent work. This is the same reasoning as the queue rule above applied to the INDEPENDENT rows: with no certified translations being obtained, no reading of a byline changes the packet, so calling those rows "unsettled" overstated the remaining work. Measured the same day, all 45 rows the dashboard had labelled "Independent but unsettled" were non-English — 42 withheld by the screen and 3 second-language copies of one German article whose English version is already highlighted (`cit-000991`, `cit-001260`, `cit-001539`) — and **0** were genuinely open.
- Collapsing them does not remove them from the status partition. `tally.js` publishes `non_english_independent` (45) for the rows that carry an INDEPENDENT classification and are held by the language screen, because `tallyEntries` and the per-article gate in `tools/check-ledger-vs-snapshot.js` must still sum to `records`: `independent + independent_pending + non_english_independent + dependent + self + review = records`. It is **not** the same set as `non_english_withheld` (42), which additionally requires a settled basis and excludes language editions because it answers "what would a translator reclaim" — do not merge the two figures. Adding the term means touching `build-ledger.js` (both row builders, the totals seed, `CSV_COLUMNS`, the global block), `build-catalog.js` `reconcile()`, `query-catalog.js` `stats()` and `build-dashboard-data.js`; a store SQL that stops matching the predicate is exactly what the reconciliation checks exist to catch.
- **A key listed twice in the ledger's totals-seed array silently doubles a global figure.** Adding `non_english_independent` on 2026-11-03 produced a global of 90 against a per-article sum of 45 because one edit had flattened two entries onto one line. Nothing failed — the seed is a list, not a set. When adding a tally figure, compare the written global against the sum of the dated CSV's rows before quoting either.
- `isHighlighted()` already refused a language-flagged row, so this rule changes **no exhibit mark** and needs no re-print; `tools/audit-highlights.js` confirms it. Expect it to move labels and bucket membership only. If a future change of this kind does move a mark, that is a separate defect.
- A change to a counting rule does not reach exhibits already captured, because each report's `status`, `confirm_state` and language flag were written once at capture time. Applying one is an offline sequence: the re-apply tool for the rule that changed (`tools/reapply-language.js --write`, or `tools/reapply-corroboration.js --write`), then `tools/reprint-exhibits.js --changed --write`, then `tools/audit-highlights.js` while nothing downstream has moved yet, then `tools/build-catalog.js --write` and **only then** `tools/build-ledger.js`, then `tools/build-review-sheet.js --md` and `tools/build-dashboard-data.js`, and finally `tools/test-pdf-fit.js`. Both re-apply tools are dry-run by default, back up what they touch, and print the mark flips; the re-printer refuses to save unless its applied mark count matches the rule. The order is not cosmetic — the audit needs the re-printed HTML but not the store, so it fails fast, and the ledger reads its rows out of the store, so rebuilding it against a stale store raises a defect and writes nothing.
- **Checking the yellow highlights.** The marks are baked into each saved exhibit HTML and printed into its PDF, so nothing downstream notices when they stop matching the rule — the ledger reads the report JSON and the PDF is only a picture. `tools/audit-highlights.js` is the check: it replays the current rule over every filed page offline (headless browser, every network request aborted, no Scholar contact), and also verifies each exhibit PDF exists and is non-empty and that no language edition is marked. It exits 1 on any disagreement. Takes about 40 seconds for all 168 pages.
- Run the audit **after every batch of decisions or rule changes, not once at the end**. A drift found in the batch that caused it names the rows involved; a drift found after a hundred more decisions has to be bisected. `tools/apply-decision.js --rebuild` runs it inside the chain, immediately after the re-print and **before** the store is rebuilt, so a disagreement stops the chain with the ledger, review sheet and dashboard all still showing the last consistent state — a packet whose figures moved while its exhibits did not is the failure worth paying an extra step to avoid. A normal decision batch is therefore already audited; do not treat a separate audit run as optional busywork after anything that bypassed that tool.
- Run `tools/audit-highlights.js` and `tools/test-pdf-fit.js` once more immediately before the exhibits are filed, as the final gate on the set being shipped. Between the last audit and filing, nothing should have changed; if anything did, audit again rather than relying on the earlier pass.
- Never conclude highlights are correct by looking at a PDF, and never "fix" a highlighted row by editing the exhibit HTML or PDF. The re-printer is the only thing that redraws an exhibit, from the rules; if the audit disagrees, the report data or the rule is wrong.
- `tools/test-pdf-fit.js` measures **the most recently modified** saved citing HTML unless a page is passed explicitly, so a pass or failure says nothing about the other pages. Pass a page, or pass `--all`. Since the 0.73 scale change on 2026-11-02 every one of the 168 filed citing exhibits prints to one sheet; the two profile exhibits (`akul-mehta-google-scholar-*.pdf`, 48 rows) are expected to run long. `tools/audit-highlights.js` now also fails on any citing exhibit PDF that prints to more than one sheet, so a future rule or content change that tips a page over is caught rather than discovered at filing.
- Per the user's rule on 2026-11-02, a preprint or `[CITATION]` entry is recorded as a duplicate of a journal record **only when it is demonstrably the same work**. A preprint server alone is not the test, and neither is a similar title. Where the titles differ, deeper evidence is required before merging — a matching complete byline plus matching venue/DOI chain, or the published paper's own statement of a prior version. Without that, the row is classified on its own merits: if its author list shares nobody with the cited work and names neither PI, it is **independent**, because it appears independent. Merging on suspicion both hides a real citation and rests on an unproven identity claim in a filing.
- The converse also holds: `tools/tally.js` `paperKey` merges rows on a normalised identical title only, so a differently-titled preprint is never auto-merged and needs the manual evidence above. When two rows are left as separate works, the distinct-paper figure counts them as two — say so plainly rather than implying the packet proves they are one paper.
- Where the evidence **does** meet that bar, record the identity with `tools/apply-decision.js --row=<uid> --same-work-as=<anchor uid> --note="..."` (the note is required — an unproven identity claim in a filing is exactly what the rule above prevents). It writes `same_work_key` on the rows and nothing else: status, confirm_state, title and the exhibit mark are untouched. `tally.foldSameWork` is the single place a fold becomes a consequence — it picks the copy that stands, points the rest at it via `duplicate_of`, and sets `duplicate_kind = 'same-work'` so a same-work fold is never blurred with a language edition. Both `groupReports` and `build-catalog.applyEditions` call it; do not reimplement it. `uniquePapers` groups on `same_work_key` when present, which is what stops a preprint and its published article counting as two papers. `--revert` takes the fold off again.
- When two rows are copies of one paper, `copyReliability` in `tools/tally.js` picks which copy the decision is taken from. A **demonstrated** overlap with the cited work outranks a clean but blind read: a copy whose author list names the PI or the former PI decides the row even when the other copy has the more complete byline, because "this person is on both papers" is evidence and "I read a complete list that happened to be silent" is not. Found on 2026-11-02 with the VCU dissertation whose author shared no name with the paper but whose advisor was the former PI — the DEPENDENT copy had been losing to an INDEPENDENT one and a self-citation was being counted.
- **A fold must stay within one cited paper.** `foldSameWork` groups on `same_work_key` alone and never compares `cites_id`, then marks the losing copies `duplicate_of` — which `isHighlighted()` refuses. So a fold that crossed cited papers would silently remove a highlight from one exhibit. The mistake is easy to make because one citing article appears on the "cited by" page of *every* paper it cites: two rows can be the same WORK while being two separate CITATIONS, and independence is relative to the cited paper. Measured 2026-11-03, **178 title-keyed groups span more than one cited paper**, so the confusion is common in this corpus. `foldProblem()` in `tools/apply-decision.js` is the gate and refuses the whole batch; it also refuses when either side has no `cites_id`, because "unknown" must never be read as "same". The 178 are correct as they stand — one distinct work, genuinely that many citations — and must never be folded.
- Adding a signal to `copyReliability`, `uniquePapers` or any tally figure means adding its inputs to **every** projection out of the store: `applyPrimaryCopy` in `tools/build-catalog.js` and `storeEntries()` in `tools/build-ledger.js`. Both compute the same numbers from copied rows, so a field left out of one makes the two disagree and the reconciliation gate fails — which is the guard working, not a bug to route around.
- Preserve the user's existing files and organization. Make narrowly scoped changes and do not silently discard or overwrite user-authored material.
- Exhibit PDFs must look like a Google Scholar results page where only confirmed independent citations are highlighted in yellow. Do not add legends, review marks, or faded rows to an exhibit; keep such annotations in the separate review notes or behind a debug flag.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-10-29, every exhibit PDF page must print a header showing the Google Scholar URL it was captured from (plus the snapshot date) and a footer with page numbers. This is the one permitted annotation; it overrides the earlier no-print-header rule.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-02, exhibit PDFs print on US Letter at **73%** scale. The original 75% (2026-10-29) left three tall citing pages printing to two sheets; the user asked for a slight reduction, and 0.73 is the highest scale measured to put every filed citing page on one sheet (0.74 still overflows). The scale, margins and format live in one module, `tools/print-settings.js`, imported by the capture, the re-printer, the profile capture and the fit test — never restate them inline, since five copies drifting apart is what let the exhibits disagree silently.
- `tools/test-pdf-fit.js` decides by counting the sheets the printed PDF actually has, not by measuring where the last result row ends. The old row-bottom arithmetic reported all 170 pages fitting while three filed exhibits were genuinely two sheets, because snippets and links below the last row's own box still print. `--all` checks every saved citing page (a few workpapers wider than the filed set) and exits 1 on any multi-sheet page. Note it still reports the most recently modified saved page unless one is passed explicitly, so a single-page pass says nothing about the others.
- Google Scholar shows 10 citing articles per page for this profile, and a `pagesize=20` parameter does not change that. Page through a citing list by following the page's own "Next" link, which carries Scholar's real step size and query parameters; hand-built `start=` offsets drop parameters such as `as_sdt`, `sciodt`, and `scipsc` and silently skip records. Expect roughly one page per 10 citations.
- Greek letters in a title are scientific notation, not evidence of a non-English paper (for example an alpha-1,2-mannosidase or beta-catenin title is English). Treat a small number of Greek letters alongside substantial Latin text as notation and do not suppress the citation; only flag it when Greek letters make up the body of the text. Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-02 this is implemented as a **share** test, not a count: `tools/capture-citations.js` flags Greek only above 25% of the letters, and a stray non-Latin character in a snippet flags only above the same share (one Cyrillic epsilon in a chemical-name abstract is a rendering artifact, not a foreign-language entry).
- A byline year is Scholar's rendering of a venue, not a verified publication date, and it is sometimes the date of a parent reference work. `cit-000036` ("Anticoagulants", DOI `10.1002/0471266949.bmc182.pub2`, a *Burger's Medicinal Chemistry* chapter Crossref-dated 2021-04-26) carries **2003** because Scholar itself prints 2003 — confirmed against the filed exhibit HTML, so it is not a capture artifact. The year chart in `tools/build-dashboard-data.js` therefore refuses a parsed date earlier than the year of the paper cited, since a citing work cannot predate its source, and publishes each exclusion in `year_anomalies` so the caption names the rows rather than letting a year vanish silently. Only a known `cited_year` may exclude a row; an empty one is unknown, not evidence.
- **Do not delete a counted citation to tidy a chart.** Removing `cit-000036` would move independent 1077 → 1076 and require exhibit page 4 to be re-printed, which is a filing decision for the user through `tools/apply-decision.js`, not a dashboard cleanup. Fixing a derived chart and changing filed evidence are different acts; when a date is wrong but the citation is real, exclude the date and say so.
- Every chart that splits a publication's records must use the same exhaustive bucket set as the waffle, with `review_queue` rather than raw `review` and the non-English rows in their own bucket, so a bar's segments add up to its record count. A stack drawn at zero still emits a legend key, which reads as hidden work — draw `independent_pending` only when some row actually has it.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-03, **every listing of citing works leads with `row_uid`**, the same `span.uid` column the review queue, unsettled and non-English tables use — including the per-work list on `works.html` and the citing-patents table on `index.html`. A row must be nameable by its permanent uid from anywhere, since a title plus exhibit page is not a stable handle. The table's search box must match on the uid too.
- **A `@media print` rule only takes effect on the shared browser page, not a freshly created one.** Setting `Emulation.setEmulatedMedia` over CDP on a `newPage()` leaves `matchMedia('print').matches` false, so a check reports `table-layout: auto` and a phantom overflow and looks like broken CSS. Emulate on the already-open page, and set the emulation *after* navigation.
- **Measure table width against the sheet whenever a column is added.** Chrome clips whatever hangs past the page edge and warns about nothing: `#patents-table` was 869px against 663px available and had been losing its last printed column silently until the uid column made it obvious. `table-layout: fixed` with weighted `th` widths in the print block is the fix already used for the other appendix tables.

## Access and Progress Tracking

- If a CAPTCHA, unusual-traffic screen, sign-in challenge, or other access wall appears, stop browsing and data collection immediately. Do not solve, bypass, or repeatedly retry the challenge. Tell the user what appeared and where work stopped, then wait for the user to clear it before resuming.
- Maintain `Independent Citation Record/Progress Tracker.json` as the working checkpoint. Update it when access, review progress, generated exhibits, or blockers change; keep the last verified step, next step, source/date, and unresolved items accurate. Do not record guesses as facts.
- Before stopping at an access wall, record the checkpoint in the tracker so the work can resume from that point.
- Do not claim a browser page was saved or printed to PDF unless an actual PDF file was produced and verified.

## Browser Automation Conduct

- Prefer the existing capture tooling in `tools/` (`capture.js`, `capture-citations.js`, `list-all-publications.js`) and its shared pacing module `tools/human.js`. Reuse these helpers rather than writing new fixed-delay navigation.
- Browse politely to reduce rate-limiting: use randomized waits, not fixed ones. Approximate guidance: 3-6s to let a page settle, 6-14s between distinct pages with occasional longer pauses, and 3-7s after actions such as "Show more". Slow is acceptable; the packet is not time-critical.
- Interact the way a person does: move the cursor in steps rather than teleporting, scroll in uneven increments with brief reading pauses, and return to the top before extracting or printing.
- Keep the request volume minimal. Fetch only the pages needed for the current step, batch related reads in one session, and never parallelize requests to the same host.
- Treat a disabled control as "busy": wait and retry at most once, then treat the list as complete. Do not hammer a button or URL in a tight retry loop.
- Reuse the persistent browser profile (`tools/.playwright-profile`) so an access grant the user already obtained carries over, reducing repeat challenges.
- Slowing down is courtesy only. 
- Use `channel:chrome` to ensure the browser automation runs with the Chrome channel, which may help maintain consistent behavior and reduce detection issues. Chrome was installed on 2026-10-29 at `C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe` and the channel resolves; `tools/human.js` still falls back to the bundled Chromium with a logged notice if it ever stops resolving, so check for that line at the start of a run rather than assuming Chrome is in use.
- When an access wall stops a run, save a dated screenshot and HTML copy of the screen into `Exhibits/Supporting` with a `BLOCKED-` prefix. These are the record of where work stopped and must never be filed alongside the exhibits in `Exhibits/PDFs`.

## Drafting and File Changes

- Use clear, professional language suitable for an immigration evidence packet. Avoid overstating the strength or significance of evidence.
- Retain source titles, author names, venues, and dates accurately. Mark uncertain details for review rather than silently normalizing them.
- Before making material changes to evidence or claims, explain the factual basis and flag any needed user or attorney confirmation.

## Improving These Instructions

- As work progresses, refine this file with durable project-specific preferences and lessons learned; keep it concise, avoid one-off details, and discuss with the user before changing or removing an existing rule.
